claims.text: High-entropy alloys can exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
The proposed transition is caused by the unique compositional complexity of high-entropy alloys.
High-entropy alloys are initially ductile at room temperature.
Exposure to a specific temperature range induces embrittlement in high-entropy alloys.
The relevant temperature range is one typically associated with temper embrittlement in conventional alloys.
High-entropy alloys possess a complex microstructure that mediates the proposed transition.
Multiple alloying elements interact at elevated temperatures.
Interactions among multiple alloying elements alter phase stability and ductility.
High-entropy alloys become brittle within the proposed temperature range.
High-entropy alloys return to ductile behavior upon cooling.
High-entropy alloys maintain ductility across a wide temperature range without embrittlement.
The proposed behavior is limited to high-entropy alloys.
The proposed behavior does not apply to conventional alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome assert embrittlement in high-entropy alloys, whereas the baseline says they maintain ductility across a wide temperature range without embrittlement; no condition clearly reconciles these statements.
The conditions invoke a temper-embrittlement range associated with conventional alloys, while the boundary says the proposed behavior does not apply to conventional alloys.
